labels.answer: Capnocytophaga species (C. ochracea, C. gingivalis, C. sputigena)

cloze.text: Necrotizing periodontal diseases (NPDs) are severe inflammatory conditions of the periodontium characterized by tissue {{c1::necrosis}} ("death"), commonly presenting with {{c2::"punched-out"}} interdental papillae.
Necrotizing periodontal diseases are strongly linked to an {{c1::impaired host immune system}}.

Clinical signs of necrotizing periodontal diseases include a {{c1::yellowish-white pseudomembrane}}, pain, spontaneous bleeding, a strong {{c2::fetid odor}}, and systemic involvement like fever or swollen lymph nodes.
cloze.extra: Board Alert: main symptoms of necrotizing conditions — PAIN, fetid odor, pseudomembrane, cratered papillae, punched-out papillae, fever, fatigue and lymphadenopathy (swollen lymph nodes). Find them in your case studies.

cloze.text: Necrotizing gingivitis (NG) affects the {{c1::gingival tissues (primarily the interdental papillae)}} only.
cloze.extra: Key characteristics: acute inflammatory process; necrosis/ulcer of interdental papillae; gingival bleeding; pain. Other signs: halitosis, pseudomembrane, regional lymphadenopathy, fever.

cloze.text: In children, necrotizing gingivitis may also present with {{c1::sialorrhea}}.
cloze.extra: Sialorrhea = excessive salivation.

cloze.text: Necrotizing gingivitis is often seen in {{c1::young adults}} (e.g., stressed college students, soldiers).
Contributing factors for necrotizing gingivitis include poor plaque control, {{c1::stress}}, fatigue, alcohol/drug use, {{c2::smoking}}, and poor nutrition.
Necrotizing periodontitis (NP) represents progression from NG with {{c1::bone involvement}}; its key sign is {{c2::rapid bone loss}}.
cloze.extra: Affects the periodontium (gingiva and underlying alveolar bone). Also: necrosis/ulceration of papillae, spontaneous bleeding, halitosis (fetid odor), pain, pseudomembrane, lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise. Shares NG's contributing factors.

cloze.text: In necrotizing stomatitis (NS), soft-tissue necrosis extends {{c1::beyond the gingiva}}; destruction may occur through the alveolar mucosa, tongue, cheek, and palate.
Necrotizing stomatitis typically occurs in {{c1::severely systemically compromised}} patients and is the {{c2::most severe}} form of necrotizing conditions.
cloze.extra: Atypical cases may develop without prior NG/NP lesions.

cloze.text: Treatment of necrotizing periodontal disease: removal of the {{c1::pseudomembrane}}, {{c2::limited debridement with an ultrasonic scaler}}, and oral hygiene instruction.
Patients with necrotizing periodontal disease should avoid irritating foods and use {{c1::chlorhexidine}} rinses; nutritional counseling and {{c2::tobacco cessation}} are also recommended.

In necrotizing periodontal disease, {{c1::systemic}} antibiotics may be used for systemic involvement (fever, lymphadenopathy) or unresponsive cases, but {{c2::local}} antibiotics are contraindicated.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: In periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease, destruction can occur {{c1::with or without}} significant biofilm.
cloze.extra: Not solely initiated by plaque biofilm.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: Systemic disorders that manifest as periodontitis affect the periodontium through altered {{c1::immune responses}}, tissue defects, or {{c2::metabolic}} changes.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: In Down syndrome, periodontal attachment loss begins in {{c1::adolescence}}; intrinsic abnormalities of the {{c2::immune system}} predispose to infection.
cloze.extra: Higher prevalence and severity of periodontal disease.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: {{c1::Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome}}, a rare genetic disorder, causes severe early-onset gingival inflammation, rapidly progressive alveolar bone loss, and early loss of {{c2::primary and permanent}} teeth.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: Congenital neutropenia is a hematologic disorder with a severe lack of {{c1::neutrophils}}; severe periodontitis, higher risk of tooth loss, and {{c2::oral ulcers}} are common.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: {{c1::Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)}}, an autoimmune disease, causes oral ulcers and increased prevalence of gingival inflammation and periodontitis.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: HIV infection increases risk for {{c1::necrotizing periodontal diseases}}, oral candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, severe aphthous ulcers, Kaposi sarcoma, and {{c2::linear gingival erythema (LGE)}}.
cloze.extra: HIV = acquired immunodeficiency that increases susceptibility to infections and oral lesions.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: Cytotoxic chemotherapeutics can cause transient or prolonged {{c1::neutropenia}}, associated with increased risk for periodontitis.
cloze.extra: Cancer drugs affect immune-cell production.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: Oral squamous cell carcinoma can mimic localized periodontal disease: localized gingival swelling or ulceration, typically in the {{c1::mandibular molar}} region, with alveolar bone loss {{c2::independent of plaque}}.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: Odontogenic tumors (from tooth-forming tissues): early lesions show localized swelling and {{c1::tooth displacement}}; late features resemble {{c2::localized periodontitis}} with bone loss independent of plaque.

cloze.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
cloze.text: {{c1::Peripheral}} giant cell granuloma is an expanding epulis-like swelling on the gingiva/alveolar mucosa; {{c2::central}} GCG occurs within the bone and causes loss of deep periodontal supporting tissue.
cloze.extra: Both can cause alveolar bone loss independently of plaque.

cloze.text: Acute periodontal diseases are {{c1::rapid-onset}} conditions characterized by pain or discomfort, tissue destruction, and {{c2::infection}}.
Acute periodontal diseases include {{c1::abscesses}}, endodontic-periodontal lesions, necrotizing periodontal disease, and {{c2::herpetic gingivostomatitis}}.
Acute periodontal lesions may be {{c1::unrelated}} to concurrent gingivitis or periodontitis, and may be localized or involve multiple sites.
Peri-implant health = absence of visual signs of inflammation and {{c1::bleeding on probing}}; it can exist around implants with normal or {{c2::reduced}} bone support.
Probing depths alone cannot define peri-implant health: healthy implants may probe deeper than {{c1::3 mm}}, but crucially without {{c2::bleeding and pus}}.
Peri-implant mucositis is characterized by {{c1::bleeding on probing}} and visual signs of inflammation; pus may also be present.
Peri-implant mucositis is primarily caused by {{c1::plaque}} and is {{c2::reversible}} with measures aimed at eliminating plaque.
cloze.extra: Limited evidence exists for non-plaque-induced peri-implant mucositis.

cloze.text: Peri-implantitis: a plaque-associated condition with inflammation in the peri-implant mucosa AND subsequent {{c1::progressive loss of supporting bone}}.
{{c1::Mobility}} of an implant is a key indicator of peri-implantitis and implant failure.

Peri-implantitis is associated with poor plaque control and a history of {{c1::severe periodontitis}}; onset may be early after placement and it progresses in a {{c2::non-linear, accelerating}} pattern.
Without baseline data, peri-implantitis is diagnosed by bone loss ≥ {{c1::3}} mm AND/OR probing depths ≥ {{c2::6}} mm with bleeding and/or suppuration.
cloze.extra: Capture baseline radiographs and probe depths after placement for monitoring.

cloze.text: Hard and soft tissue implant-site deficiencies: diminished dimensions of the alveolar process/ridge resulting from {{c1::normal healing after tooth loss}}.
cloze.extra: Leads to both hard (bone) and soft (gingival) tissue deficiencies.

cloze.text: Larger ridge deficiencies can result from severe loss of periodontal support, {{c1::extraction trauma}}, endodontic infections, root fractures, {{c2::thin buccal bone plates}}, poor tooth position, injury, and {{c3::pneumatization of the maxillary sinuses}}.
Other contributing factors to implant-site deficiencies: medications and systemic diseases that reduce bone, tooth {{c1::agenesis}}, and pressure from {{c2::prostheses}}.
Periodontal disease is {{c1::multifactorial}}: affected by plaque, host response, and risk factors.
{{c1::Plaque biofilm}} and its bacteria are the main causes of periodontal disease.
Bacteria associated with periodontitis are gram-{{c1::negative}}, {{c2::motile}}, {{c3::anaerobic}}, and {{c4::rod}}-shaped.
Pathogenic biofilm is a {{c1::prerequisite}} for periodontitis, but its presence alone is {{c2::insufficient}} to cause the disease.
cloze.extra: The presence of bacteria alone is not sufficient to cause periodontal disease.

cloze.text: The {{c1::host factor}} theory: an individual's body response to bacteria dictates disease initiation and progression.
Porphyromonas gingivalis: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::key pathogen in periodontitis}}; {{c3::red}} complex.
Fusobacterium nucleatum: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::bridge organism in plaque biofilm}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
Tannerella forsythia: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::implicated in advanced periodontitis}}; {{c3::red}} complex.
Treponema denticola: {{c1::gram-negative spirochete}}; role: {{c2::motile anaerobe associated with necrotizing gingivitis}}; {{c3::red}} complex.
cloze.extra: The book says 'NUG' — necrotizing gingivitis (NG) is the AAP 2017 term.

cloze.text: Prevotella intermedia: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::associated with hormonal gingivitis and periodontitis}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
cloze.extra: The book says 'chronic periodontitis'; AAP 2017 classification (used on the NBDHE): the old terms 'chronic' and 'aggressive' periodontitis are replaced by one category, 'periodontitis', described by stage and grade.

cloze.text: Campylobacter rectus: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::associated with 'aggressive' periodontitis (pre-2017 term)}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
cloze.extra: 'Aggressive periodontitis' is the book's (pre-2017) term; AAP 2017 classification (used on the NBDHE): the old terms 'chronic' and 'aggressive' periodontitis are replaced by one category, 'periodontitis', described by stage and grade.

cloze.text: Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans (Aa): {{c1::gram-negative rod/coccobacillus (depending on conditions)}}; role: {{c2::linked to 'aggressive' periodontitis (pre-2017 term)}}; {{c3::green}} complex.
cloze.extra: 'Aggressive periodontitis' is the book's (pre-2017) term; AAP 2017 classification (used on the NBDHE): the old terms 'chronic' and 'aggressive' periodontitis are replaced by one category, 'periodontitis', described by stage and grade.

cloze.text: Eikenella corrodens: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::anaerobe found in subgingival plaque}}; {{c3::green}} complex.
Fusobacterium periodonticum: {{c1::gram-negative rod}}; role: {{c2::in biofilm, associated with gingivitis and periodontitis}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
Capnocytophaga species (C. ochracea, C. gingivalis, C. sputigena): {{c1::gram-negative rods}}; role: {{c2::involved in periodontitis (book: 'chronic')}}; {{c3::green}} complex.
cloze.extra: AAP 2017 classification (used on the NBDHE): the old terms 'chronic' and 'aggressive' periodontitis are replaced by one category, 'periodontitis', described by stage and grade.

cloze.text: Veillonella parvula: {{c1::gram-negative cocci}}; role: {{c2::'bridging organism' in oral biofilms, aids development of periodontitis}}; {{c3::purple}} complex.
Streptococcus sanguinis: {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; role: {{c2::early colonizer with a protective role in plaque biofilm}}; {{c3::yellow}} complex.
Streptococcus mitis: {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; role: {{c2::initial tooth colonizer, early plaque developer}}; {{c3::yellow}} complex.
Actinomyces naeslundii: {{c1::gram-positive rod}}; role: {{c2::root surface colonizer, early plaque developer}}; {{c3::blue}} complex.
Actinomyces viscosus: {{c1::gram-positive rod}}; role: {{c2::associated with root caries; normal oral flora}}; {{c3::blue}} complex.
Peptostreptococcus micros: {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; role: {{c2::associated with periodontal disease}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
Actinomyces odontolyticus: {{c1::gram-positive rod}}; role: {{c2::found in dental biofilm, contributes to caries and periodontitis}}; {{c3::purple}} complex.
Streptococcus constellatus: {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; role: {{c2::normal oral flora associated with periodontal disease and periodontal abscesses}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
Streptococcus oralis: {{c1::gram-positive cocci}}; role: {{c2::normal oral flora of healthy plaque}}; {{c3::yellow}} complex.
Actinomyces israelii: {{c1::gram-positive rod}}; role: {{c2::root surface colonizer; normal oral flora}}; {{c3::blue}} complex.
Eubacterium nodatum: {{c1::gram-positive rod}}; role: {{c2::associated with periodontitis and deep periodontal pockets}}; {{c3::orange}} complex.
Local risk factor — {{c1::dental calculus}}: hardened plaque that promotes bacterial retention.
Local risk factor — poorly contoured restorations: include {{c1::overhangs}} that create plaque traps and make cleaning difficult.
Local risk factors: caries (irregular surfaces promote bacterial accumulation) and irregular tooth morphology such as {{c1::grooves and concavities}} that are difficult to clean.
Local risk factor — {{c1::furcations}}: anatomical complexities in multi-rooted teeth that are difficult to access for hygiene.
Local risk factor — impingement on the {{c1::biological width}}: restorations placed too close to the crestal bone can lead to periodontal destruction.
Tobacco use is a significant risk factor: it inhibits {{c1::collagen production}}, slows healing, and can {{c2::mask inflammation}} due to impaired vascularization.
Genetics (non-modifiable): some individuals are more susceptible, e.g., severe periodontitis in {{c1::Down syndrome}} patients.
Elderly patients have higher periodontal disease rates due to associated factors (reduced dexterity, medications, osteoporosis), {{c1::not age itself}}.
Stress is a modifiable risk factor because it impairs the {{c1::immune system}}, making it harder to fight infections.
Obesity/poor nutrition compromise the immune system and tissue health; deficiencies in essential nutrients include {{c1::vitamin C}} and protein.
Diabetes mellitus increases {{c1::glucose in gingival crevicular fluid}} (bacterial nutrition), leading to delayed healing and increased infection risk.
cloze.extra: Modifiable via management.

cloze.text: Cancer treatment side effects: xerostomia, {{c1::mucositis}}, infections, loss of taste, and {{c2::bone necrosis}}.
cloze.extra: Non-modifiable (treatment).

cloze.text: Hormonal changes (pregnancy, oral contraceptives, menopause) increase gingival {{c1::sensitivity to local irritants}}.
cloze.extra: Partially modifiable.

cloze.text: Medication-induced conditions: {{c1::xerostomia}} worsens caries risk; gingival {{c2::enlargement}} is caused by anti-seizure meds, immunosuppressants, and calcium channel blockers.
cloze.extra: Modifiable via management.

cloze.text: Parafunctional habits — clenching, grinding ({{c1::bruxism}}), and {{c2::tongue thrusting}} — exert excessive stress on the periodontium, weakening it.
Mouth breathing {{c1::dries out}} the gingival tissues, increasing susceptibility to inflammation.
Occlusal trauma does NOT {{c1::initiate}} periodontitis, but it may lead to alveolar bone resorption and can {{c2::worsen pre-existing}} periodontitis.
cloze.extra: Weak evidence that it increases connective tissue loss when plaque-induced periodontitis is present.

cloze.text: Disease extent: {{c1::localized}} = less than 30% of sites (teeth) affected; {{c2::generalized}} = 30% or more.
cloze.extra: The book prints 'Localized: 30% or less' and 'Generalized: 30% or more' (overlapping at 30%). AAP 2017 standard: localized <30% of teeth, generalized ≥30%.

cloze.text: An {{c1::inactive}} disease site is stable; an {{c2::active}} disease site is currently undergoing destruction.
Embrasure space classifications are {{c1::normal, class I, class II, class III, or class IV}}.
Normal embrasure: the interdental papilla {{c1::fills the space}}; cleaning aid: {{c2::traditional dental floss}}.
Class I embrasure: tip of the papilla is apical to the {{c1::contact point}}, but the interproximal CEJ is {{c2::not visible}}; cleaning aid: traditional floss.
Class II embrasure: tip of the papilla is at or apical to the {{c1::interproximal CEJ}}, but coronal to the {{c2::facial CEJ}}.
cloze.extra: Aids: tufted dental floss, interdental brush, wooden interdental cleaner, or toothpick.

cloze.text: Class III embrasure: {{c1::complete loss of the papilla}} — the papilla is at or apical to the level of the {{c2::facial CEJ}}.
cloze.extra: Aids: tufted dental floss, interdental brush, wooden interdental cleaner, end-tuft brush, or toothpick.

basic.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
basic.front: Key distinction: periodontitis MODIFIED by a factor (smoking, hormones, diabetes) vs periodontitis as a MANIFESTATION of systemic disease?
basic.back: Modifying factors: biofilm must be present. Manifestation of systemic disease: periodontitis occurs with or without biofilm.
basic.extra: Board Alert: for 'periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease' look for genetic immune disorders, severe early onset, unusual destruction with minimal plaque, extreme cases in pediatric patients.

basic.front: Key difference between acute periodontal conditions and classic periodontal disease?
basic.back: Acute conditions can be intensely painful and often make the patient seek emergency care; immediate intervention is needed to prevent worsening and further damage.
The study of all factors that may be involved in the development of a disease
Injury from excessive forces on a tooth with NORMAL periodontal support (e.g., a high restoration)
Injury from normal or excessive forces on a tooth with REDUCED periodontal support
Papilla is enlarged and bulges out of the interproximal space
Papilla is flat and does not fill the interproximal space
Papilla has a concave depression, described as "scooped out"
Only the interdental papilla is inflamed
Only the gingival margin is inflamed
Gingival margin, papilla, and attached gingiva are inflamed
New signs of destruction reappear after periodontal therapy, caused by inadequate professional care or self-care
Destruction continues despite appropriate professional care and self-care
Open space apical to the contact area; covered by the interdental papilla in health

basic.front: Which embrasure classes can be cleaned with traditional dental floss?
basic.extra: Class II and III: tufted floss, interdental brush, wooden interdental cleaner, toothpick (Class III also end-tuft brush).

mcq.question: A 21-year-old college student in exam week presents with painful, bleeding gums, punched-out interdental papillae covered by a grey-white pseudomembrane, and a fetid odor. Radiographs show no bone loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Papillary necrosis, pain, pseudomembrane and fetid odor in a stressed young adult = necrotizing gingivitis. Necrotizing periodontitis would show (rapid) bone loss; necrotizing stomatitis spreads beyond the gingiva.

mcq.question: All of the following are appropriate in managing necrotizing gingivitis EXCEPT one. Which is the EXCEPTION?
mcq.explanation: Local antibiotics are contraindicated in necrotizing periodontal disease; systemic antibiotics are reserved for systemic involvement or unresponsive cases. The other choices are standard treatment.

mcq.section: Periodontitis as a manifestation of systemic disease
mcq.question: A 4-year-old has severe gingival inflammation, rapidly progressive alveolar bone loss and is already losing primary teeth despite little plaque. Which condition is most likely?
mcq.explanation: Papillon-Lefèvre is a rare genetic disorder with severe early-onset inflammation, rapid bone loss and early loss of primary AND permanent teeth. In Down syndrome attachment loss typically begins in adolescence.

mcq.question: Which patient complaint is most typical of an ACUTE periodontal condition rather than classic chronic periodontal disease?
options: C. Intense pain prompting an emergency visit
mcq.answer: C. Intense pain prompting an emergency visit
mcq.explanation: Acute periodontal lesions are rapid-onset and can be intensely painful — the key difference from classic periodontal disease, which is usually painless.

mcq.question: An implant placed 3 years ago bleeds and suppurates on probing; probing depth is 7 mm and the radiograph shows 4 mm of bone loss. No baseline records exist. What is the diagnosis?
mcq.explanation: Without baseline data, bone loss ≥3 mm and/or PD ≥6 mm with bleeding/suppuration = peri-implantitis. Mucositis shows bleeding and inflammation without the progressive bone loss that defines peri-implantitis, and is reversible.

mcq.question: Which bacterium is considered the key pathogen in periodontitis and belongs to the red complex?
mcq.explanation: P. gingivalis (gram-negative rod, red complex) is the key pathogen. F. nucleatum is the orange-complex bridge organism; S. sanguinis and A. viscosus are early colonizers/normal flora.

mcq.question: Which of the following periodontal risk factors is NON-modifiable?
mcq.explanation: Genetics (e.g., Down syndrome) cannot be changed. Diabetes is modifiable via management; tobacco and overhangs can be eliminated.

mcq.question: A tooth with 50% bone loss from past periodontitis becomes mobile under normal chewing forces. This is best described as:
mcq.explanation: Secondary occlusal trauma = normal or excessive forces on a tooth with REDUCED support. Primary occlusal trauma involves excessive forces on a tooth with normal support (e.g., a high restoration).

mcq.question: Despite thorough scaling and root planing and excellent home care, a patient's pockets continue to deepen. This is best described as:
mcq.explanation: Refractory = destruction continues despite appropriate professional care AND self-care. Recurrent = disease returns after therapy because of inadequate care.

mcq.question: The tip of the interdental papilla is apical to the interproximal CEJ but coronal to the facial CEJ. Which class of embrasure, and which aid is appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Class II: papilla at/apical to the interproximal CEJ but coronal to the facial CEJ; aids are tufted floss, interdental brush, wooden cleaner or toothpick. Class I still allows traditional floss but the CEJ isn't visible.
